answer.rationale: The binding constraint is stated in the objective: reduce TCO WITHOUT increasing delivery risk. The line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract dies in 14 days, so any decision that puts first-article qualification, tooling transfer, or logistics ramp on the critical path inside two weeks is the highest-variance option available, regardless of quoted price. memory_c2 is the memory that most tempts a full switch, so it is the first thing I verify: I need the original record to see what volume share, part criticality, and ramp window that switch actually covered, whether it was a like-for-like primary migration or a secondary/low-criticality line, and whether 'quick onboarding' was measured under slack capacity rather than at 94% utilization. A cost win recorded under slack conditions does not transfer to a no-buffer cliff, and the consolidated summary hides exactly those qualifiers. I verify memory_c6 second because it defines whether a cost lever exists that does not require migration: the incumbent has refused to reopen PRICE this cycle, but term length and payment terms are a distinct lever (memory_c4 recovered margin on both price and terms via benchmarking). If c6's source shows the volume-pricing discount was material and mechanically tied to commitment length rather than to a mid-cycle price concession, negotiating a term-and-terms restructure is the only path that both secures continuity past day 85 and moves cost. So my intended action is negotiate_terms, executed guarded: a short bridge extension that removes the 14-day cliff, paired with a benchmarked multi-year/volume-and-payment-terms proposal, while formally qualifying the low-cost vendor as a second source (memory_c3's dual-source lesson) for the NEXT review rather than this one. Stated uncertainty and risk: (1) I do not yet know that term restructuring reaches 18%; it may close only part of the gap, and I am explicitly not claiming the mandate is met by this action. (2) The downstream value risk is real and runs both ways: locking a multi-year commitment to buy near-term continuity can trade away the leverage and exit optionality that the low-cost quote currently gives us, and can quietly become the reason a future cycle cannot switch at all. Conversely, if verification shows c6's discount was thin or conditioned on scope we no longer need, the honest read is that the mandate cannot be met this cycle without accepting migration risk, and that gap should be escalated to finance as a real conflict between the 18% target and the no-added-delivery-risk constraint rather than papered over by a rushed switch. (3) If c2's source record shows the vendor was in fact proven at comparable volume and criticality with a ramp shorter than the runway, I will revise toward a staged dual-source split instead of defending my initial call.
